stories.title: Will Haze Spoil Singapore's Big Outdoor Events Again?
stories.headline_kid: Singapore might get smoky skies again soon, and organisers of big events like the F1 night race are already making backup plans.
summary: Every year around this time, dry weather in Indonesia can cause forest and peatland fires, especially on the island of Borneo. Smoke from these fires sometimes travels across the sea on the wind and reaches Singapore. We call this smoky, hazy air 'haze', and it can make the sky look grey and the air harder to breathe.

This year, experts say the fire season could be one of the worst in years because of a weather pattern called El Niño, which makes the region drier than usual. That is worrying news because Singapore has several huge outdoor events planned soon, including the famous Formula 1 night race, which draws huge crowds who sit outside for hours.

Because of this, people organising outdoor events are already preparing 'contingency plans' — that just means backup plans in case something goes wrong. This could include watching air quality readings closely, having indoor areas ready, handing out masks, or even changing event timings if the haze gets too bad.
This has happened before in Singapore, so many families already know the drill: checking the PSI (Pollutant Standards Index) app, keeping windows closed, and having an N95 mask ready just in case.

lenses.me: If the haze gets bad, you might need to stay indoors during recess or skip outdoor PE lessons — so it's smart to know how to check the air quality yourself.
lenses.family: Your family might need to change weekend outdoor plans, like a park visit or a barbecue, if the haze rolls in.
lenses.friends: School sports days or outdoor CCAs could be moved indoors or postponed if the air becomes unhealthy.
lenses.nation: Singapore has to prepare backup plans for major events like the F1 race, which brings in tourists and money, so haze is a real headache for organisers.
lenses.world: Haze shows how countries in Southeast Asia share the same air — fires far away in Indonesia can still affect the sky above Singapore.

stories.title: Why Petrol and Bus Fares Might Get Pricier Soon
stories.headline_kid: A ceasefire between the US and Iran has ended, and oil prices are shooting up — which could make everyday things cost more in Singapore.
summary: A 'ceasefire' is like a timeout in a fight, where both sides agree to stop attacking each other for a while. The United States and Iran had one, but it just ended, and Iran has warned it might act even more aggressively. This has made people around the world nervous.

Whenever there is tension in the Middle East, a region that supplies a lot of the world's oil, prices for oil tend to rise quickly. Oil is not just for cars — it's used to make plastic, run ships and planes, and even generate electricity.

Singapore does not have its own oil, so we buy almost everything from overseas. When oil becomes more expensive to buy, it can cost more to ship goods here, power our homes, and fill up cars and buses — which sometimes leads to higher prices for things like transport and daily goods.
Investors around the world also got jittery, causing financial markets to wobble. While this sounds complicated, the simple idea is: trouble far away can still affect prices closer to home.

lenses.me: You might hear grown-ups talking about rising petrol or bus fares at the dinner table because of this news.
lenses.family: Your family may need to be more careful with spending if daily costs like transport or electricity go up.
lenses.friends: You and your friends might notice snack or bus fare prices creeping up over time.
lenses.nation: Singapore's economy is closely linked to global oil prices since we import almost everything we use.
lenses.world: Conflicts in one part of the world, like the Middle East, can affect prices and economies everywhere, showing how connected countries are.

stories.title: Why Are Some Singaporeans Quitting Their Regular Jobs?
stories.headline_kid: More adults in Singapore are leaving their normal office jobs to try something different — and everyone is curious why.
summary: Many companies today are cutting jobs because of automation and AI (Artificial Intelligence), which can do some tasks that people used to do. This makes many workers feel unsure about how safe their jobs are — this is called 'job insecurity'.

Because of this worry, some Singaporeans are choosing to leave their regular 9-to-5 jobs and try new things instead — like starting a small online business, becoming a full-time content creator, or opening a food stall. This is sometimes called a 'side hustle' when done part-time, or a full career change when done completely.

People find these stories fascinating because they seem brave and hopeful, especially at a time when many feel nervous about layoffs. Social media is full of stories of people who 'walked away' from safe jobs to follow their passions.

This trend shows how ideas about work and money are changing. In the past, many people believed studying hard would guarantee a stable job for life — but with fast-changing technology, more people are rethinking what a 'good job' really means.

lenses.me: It's worth thinking early about what kind of work excites you, since jobs in the future may look very different from today.
lenses.family: Your parents might be having conversations at home about job security or trying something new for extra income.
lenses.friends: You and your classmates might talk about dream jobs, and some might already dream of starting their own businesses.
lenses.nation: Singapore's workforce needs to keep adapting as technology changes what kinds of jobs exist.
lenses.world: This is part of a bigger, global trend where AI and automation are changing how people think about work everywhere, not just in Singapore.

stories.title: Indonesia Tries to Make It Rain to Stop Huge Fires
stories.headline_kid: Indonesia is spraying chemicals into clouds to make it rain, hoping to put out fires that could send haze to Singapore.
summary: In Indonesia's Borneo island, huge fires have been burning through forests and peatlands — areas of wet, spongy ground packed with plant material that can catch fire and smoulder for a long time. Experts say this year's fire season could be one of the worst in years, because a weather pattern called El Niño is making the region drier than usual.

To fight the fires, scientists are trying something called 'cloud seeding'. This means flying planes into clouds and spraying special chemicals that help raindrops form faster, hoping to trigger rain that can put out the flames. It is not usually used to fight fires, so this is a fairly new and hopeful experiment.

This matters to Singapore because when these fires burn, they release thick smoke that can travel across the sea and cause haze here, making our air unhealthy to breathe. This is the same haze problem that worries event organisers in Singapore, including those preparing for outdoor events like the F1 race.
It's still uncertain if cloud seeding will fully solve the fire problem, and environmentalists are watching closely to see if it works and if it's safe for nature.

lenses.me: If the haze gets bad because of these fires, you might need to stay indoors during recess or PE lessons.
lenses.family: Families might need to buy air purifiers or masks if the haze crosses over to Singapore.
lenses.friends: Outdoor sports and school events with friends could be affected if the smoke drifts here.
lenses.nation: Singapore often works with Indonesia and other neighbours to monitor and manage haze problems together.
lenses.world: This story shows how climate patterns like El Niño can cause serious problems that cross borders and affect many countries at once.

stories.title: Lions Win a Historic Match — But Still Get Knocked Out
stories.headline_kid: Singapore's football team beat Thailand for the first time in about 14 years — but still lost the overall tie and got knocked out of the tournament.
summary: Singapore's national football team, nicknamed the Lions, faced Thailand in the semi-finals of the ASEAN Football Championship. This is one of the biggest football competitions in Southeast Asia, where national teams compete for glory.

In the second match (called the 'second leg'), the Lions pulled off an impressive win against Thailand — their first victory over this tough rival in about 14 years! That's an incredible achievement, since Thailand has been one of the strongest teams in the region.

However, football semi-finals like this are often decided over two matches, and the two scores are added together — this total is called the 'aggregate' score. Even though Singapore won the second match, Thailand had won by more in the first match, so the aggregate score ended 3-4 in Thailand's favour.

This meant Singapore was eliminated from the tournament, even after such a memorable win. Fans praised the team's fighting spirit and hope this victory is a sign of good things to come for Singapore football in the future.

lenses.me: This story is a great reminder that trying your best matters, even if you don't win in the end.
lenses.family: Your family might have cheered together while watching the match on TV or online.
lenses.friends: You and your classmates might be talking about the exciting win at school, even though the team was eliminated.
lenses.nation: This win boosts national pride and shows Singapore football is improving, even in a tough loss overall.
lenses.world: It highlights the competitive football rivalry between Southeast Asian nations like Singapore and Thailand.
